description:
Learn Python by building tools for everyday tasks.

This beginner-friendly guide takes you from basic syntax to twelve practical automation projects: tracking expenses, managing to-do lists and shopping budgets, organizing files and photos, finding duplicate files, recording habits and reminders, checking the weather, comparing prices, searching notes, and exploring an AI-assisted note workflow.

title: Getting AI to Do Things：A Practical Guide to Clear Instructions and Reliable Workflows
status: 在 Google Play 開始販售
subtitle: A Practical Guide to Clear Instructions and Reliable Workflows
description:
AI can produce a polished answer and still miss the point, fill in details you never supplied, or give you something that is difficult to use. The answer is not to search for a magic prompt. It is to make the task clear, provide the right context and source material, set useful constraints, and decide in advance what a good deliverable must include.

This practical guide introduces a six-part task brief: goal, context, source material, constraints, deliverable, and acceptance criteria. Through examples and exercises, it shows how to choose suitable tasks, handle missing information, break larger work into manageable stages, give specific feedback, check important claims, and build repeatable workflows.

The book also explains why a fluent answer is not proof of accuracy, why sensitive data and third-party material require care, and why external or high-stakes actions need appropriate human approval. Its examples are teaching illustrations—not evidence that a particular AI tool will always follow instructions or produce a correct result.

Written for general readers using AI in work, learning, and everyday tasks, the book assumes no programming background. It does not promise that any prompt guarantees correctness or that AI replaces human judgment. AI output may be incomplete or wrong; people remain responsible for decisions, and specialist questions should go to qualified professionals.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a shared interface for discovering and using those capabilities. Build a small local TypeScript server, then use guided examples and architecture exercises to understand how a larger assistant could work. description:
Asking an AI agent to “finish the work” is easy. Getting files you can inspect, steps you can repeat, and evidence you can trust takes a deliberate workflow.

This practical guide introduces the Pi Coding Agent and distinguishes it from Oh My Pi, a separate fork. It shows you how to build and assess Skills, define multi-agent handoffs, choose models for specific tasks, and design rule-based routing without treating model output as proof of success.

The final six chapters follow a book-production project from audience and outline through drafting, diagrams, review, a publication candidate, and long-term maintenance. Each chapter includes examples, operating guidance, common failure modes, checklists, and an offline exercise workbook. The book keeps documented behavior, local checks, and untested assumptions separate, so you can tell what the evidence supports.

You do not need to be a programmer, but you should be comfortable using a terminal, reading command output, and managing files. Live model use requires your own provider account and may incur charges. Product commands, model availability, prices, and platform rules can change; verify them for your version and region.

description:
A website can begin with a single sentence. Turning that idea into a reliable, maintainable site takes clear requirements, sound tool choices, careful testing, and a plan for what happens after launch.

This practical guide walks you through the full process. Learn how websites and APIs work, compare no-code, CMS, AI-assisted, and code-based approaches, and use AI to plan pages, build features, and troubleshoot problems. Follow a running project from its first page through deployment and ongoing maintenance. Then explore how to add AI features with clear limits for data, security, cost, and responsibility.

You will learn to:

• Turn vague ideas into small tasks with observable acceptance criteria.

• Choose tools based on your requirements, constraints, and evidence.

• Review AI-generated code instead of trusting a polished-looking result.

• Prepare a site for deployment, protect secrets, and test production workflows.

• Maintain a live site through monitoring, backups, updates, and recovery plans.

• Add AI features while considering privacy, reliability, cost, and user safety.

Designed for curious beginners, website owners, independent builders, and developers who want a practical framework for working with AI. Companion prompts, checklists, and exercises are available in the linked GitHub repository.
